Class Enumeration Using Predictive Surprisal

pmc_surprisal.Rd

Compares random-effects mixture meta-analysis models using simulation-based predictive surprisal. For each candidate model, repeated datasets are simulated, and kernel density estimation (KDE) is used to evaluate the surprisal of the observed effect sizes under the simulated distribution.

Usage

pmc_surprisal(x, ..., reps = 100L, ci = 0.95, nboot = 100L)

Arguments

x

A list of at least two fitted remix models, typically representing different numbers of latent classes. All models must be fitted to the same observed effect sizes.

...

Additional arguments passed to surprisal().

reps

Integer. Number of simulated datasets generated for each candidate model. Defaults to 100.

ci

Numeric. Confidence level for the bootstrap confidence intervals of differences in mean surprisal. Defaults to 0.95.

nboot

Integer. Number of bootstrap replications used to estimate confidence intervals for differences in mean surprisal. Defaults to 100.

Value

A data.frame of class pmc_df containing:

comparison

Comparison type: dif_seq or dif_one.

null

Name of the reference model.

alt

Name of the alternative model.

null_stat

Mean simulated-data surprisal for the reference model.

alt_stat

Mean simulated-data surprisal for the alternative model.

difference

Difference in mean surprisal (alt_stat - null_stat).

lb

Lower bootstrap confidence limit.

ub

Upper bootstrap confidence limit.

sig

An asterisk (*) if the upper confidence limit is below zero; otherwise an empty string.

Details

For each candidate model, the function generates reps simulated datasets.

For each simulated dataset, surprisal() estimates the distribution of the simulated effect sizes using kernel density estimation and evaluates the surprisal of the observed effect sizes under this distribution.

The mean surprisal across simulated datasets is used as a measure of predictive discrepancy. Smaller values indicate that the simulated distributions assign greater density to the observed effect sizes and therefore provide a better approximation to the observed data.

Two types of model comparisons are performed:

dif_seq

Compares each model with the preceding model in the supplied list.

dif_one

Compares each model with the first model in the supplied list.

For each comparison, the difference is calculated as the mean surprisal of the alternative model minus the mean surprisal of the reference model:

$$\Delta = \bar{S}_{alt} - \bar{S}_{null}$$

Negative differences favor the alternative model.

Confidence intervals are obtained using a nonparametric percentile bootstrap. The simulated surprisal scores for the two models are independently resampled with replacement, and the difference in their means is recalculated for each bootstrap replication.

A comparison is marked with an asterisk (*) when the upper confidence limit is below zero, indicating that the alternative model has significantly lower mean surprisal at the specified confidence level.

If the future.apply package is installed, simulations are evaluated using future.apply::future_replicate(), allowing parallel execution when an appropriate future plan has been configured. Otherwise, the function uses sequential replication.

The function uses random simulation and bootstrap resampling. Use set.seed() for reproducibility.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
library(metamixture)

set.seed(123)

# Simulate meta-analytic data
dat <- sim_remix_fixed_tau(k = 100, es = 2)

# Fit candidate models
models <- lapply(1:3, function(k) {
remix(
  yi = dat$yi,
  vi = dat$vi,
  classes = k,
  tau2 = "equal"
)
})

# Compare models using predictive surprisal
pmc <- pmc_surprisal(
models,
reps = 100,
nboot = 500
)

# Model comparisons
pmc

# Simulated surprisal scores
head(attr(pmc, "scores"))
} # }
